name: Georgia
summary_text: Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament passed the Russia-style law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region's harshest legislative package outside Russia itself. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi apartment; mourners and AP drew a direct line between the law's rhetoric and the killing. This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases, still unimplemented). Georgia's visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted. For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors.

sources.title: Trans woman killed in Georgia day after anti-LGBT law passed
sources.claim_summary: BBC (Sept 2024): trans model and influencer Kesaria Abramidze, 37, one of Georgia's best-known trans women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi flat one day after parliament passed the sweeping anti-LGBT 'Protection of Family Values and Minors' bill (84-0). Rights groups linked the killing to the government's promotion of the law; the President called it 'horrendous'. The law bans same-sex marriage, gender-affirming surgeries, adoption by non-heterosexuals, and 'promotion' of same-sex relationships in schools.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Georgia's anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation' — after the stabbing death of trans actress-model Kesaria Abramidze, Russia-style 'gay propaganda' laws stoke fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Georgia: the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

sources.title: 2024 Report to the CM of the Council of Europe on the Implementation of Decisions Related to LGBTI Rights in Georgia
sources.claim_summary: WISG et al. report (Aug 2024) to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on implementation of the Identoba group of ECtHR judgments (Aghdgomelashvili and Japaridze; WISG and Others v. Georgia): ineffective investigations into police misconduct and failure to protect demonstrators from homophobic/transphobic violence; risk of statutes of limitations expiring; new regressive anti-LGBTI legislative initiatives.

IWPR Global Voices (May 2012): 'Georgian Laws Discriminate on Transgender Rights' - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity doesn't match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers in Georgia.

OMCT/HRIDC report (May 2003) on the Rights of the Child in Georgia for the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child: covers discrimination, torture protections, violence and sexual abuse, juvenile justice - general human-rights context including institutionalisation.

sources.title: Interior Ministry says holding Tbilisi Pride is ‘impossible’ in planned locations
sources.claim_summary: OC Media (June 2019): Georgia's Interior Ministry declared holding Tbilisi Pride 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks'; organisers reported pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel; far-right groups had vowed to thwart Georgia's first Pride - state obstruction of LGBT assembly.
